In six days God speaks the heavens and earth into being, orders light and land and living things, and crowns His work by making man in His own image; on the seventh day He rests.
Adam and Eve in Eden / The Fall of Man

God plants a garden eastward in Eden and forms Eve from Adam's side as a help meet for him. But the serpent's lie unravels their innocence, and by one act of disobedience sin and shame enter the world.
Cain and Abel / The Line of Cain; Lamech's Boast
Cain, refusing God's warning, murders his brother Abel and is driven out a fugitive. His proud line multiplies in the earth, and Lamech boasts of vengeance seventy and sevenfold.
Enoch Walks with God / Sons of God and Daughters of Men
Enoch walks with God and is taken, not seeing death. But as men multiply, wickedness fills the earth, and God's Spirit will not always strive with man.
Grieved that He made man, God resolves to blot out the earth with a flood—yet Noah finds grace in His eyes. Warned of things not seen, Noah builds the ark and enters as the rains begin.
The waters prevail and every living thing outside the ark perishes, but God remembers Noah. The flood abates, the ark rests on Ararat, and a dove returns with an olive leaf of hope.
The Rainbow Covenant / Noah's Drunkenness; Canaan Cursed / The Tower of Babel

God sets His bow in the cloud as a covenant that He will never again destroy the earth by water. Yet sin remains: Noah is shamed in his drunkenness, and at Babel proud men build a tower until God scatters their tongues.
The Call of Abram / Abram and Sarai in Egypt / Abram and Lot Separate

God calls Abram to leave country and kindred for a land He will show him, promising to make of him a great nation. Famine drives him to Egypt where fear leads him to deceive, and strife over pasture parts him from Lot.
When raiders carry Lot away, Abram arms his household and rescues him. Returning victorious, he is met by Melchizedek, priest of the most high God, and pays him tithes of all.
The Covenant of the Stars / Hagar and the Birth of Ishmael
God cuts a covenant with Abram, counting his faith for righteousness and promising seed as the stars. Impatient for the promise, Sarai gives Hagar to Abram, and Ishmael is born.
The Covenant of Circumcision / Three Visitors; Sarah Laughs / Abraham Intercedes for Sodom
God seals His covenant with circumcision and renews the promise of a son to aged Sarah, who laughs. When the LORD reveals Sodom's doom, Abraham pleads for the righteous within it.
The Destruction of Sodom; Lot's Wife / Lot and His Daughters
Fire and brimstone fall upon Sodom and Gomorrah, but the angels draw Lot out. His wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt, and Lot's daughters bring forth Moab and Ammon in the cave.
Abraham and Abimelech / The Birth of Isaac; Hagar and Ishmael Cast Out / The Treaty at Beersheba
Abraham again calls Sarah his sister before Abimelech, yet God guards His promise. At the set time Isaac is born and laughter fills the tent; Hagar and Ishmael are sent away but not forsaken.
Abraham Offers Isaac / The Death and Burial of Sarah
God tests Abraham, bidding him offer Isaac upon Moriah; his hand is stayed and a ram is provided in the thicket. Sarah dies, and Abraham buys the cave of Machpelah to bury her.
Abraham sends his servant to find a bride for Isaac from his own kindred. Guided by prayer at the well, he meets Rebekah, whose willing 'I will go' brings her to Isaac for a wife.
The Death of Abraham / Jacob and Esau; the Birthright Sold / Isaac and the Wells; Abimelech
Abraham dies full of years and is gathered to his people. Esau despises and sells his birthright for a mess of pottage, while Isaac, like his father, digs wells and dwells at peace with Abimelech.
At Rebekah's urging, Jacob deceives his blind father and steals the blessing meant for Esau. Esau's bitter cry cannot recall it, and Jacob must flee his brother's murderous wrath.
Jacob's Ladder at Bethel / Jacob, Leah, and Rachel
At Bethel Jacob dreams of a ladder set up to heaven, and God renews the covenant to him. Coming to Haran, he loves Rachel and serves seven years, but Laban gives him Leah instead.
Working a second seven years for Rachel, Jacob's household grows as Leah, Rachel, and their handmaids bear him sons. God remembers the unloved and opens the barren womb.
By cunning and by God's blessing, Jacob's flocks increase greatly at Laban's expense. What Laban means for gain, the LORD turns to Jacob's prospering.
Jacob Flees; Laban Pursues / Jacob Wrestles with God at Peniel
Jacob flees homeward with his household, and Laban pursues but is warned by God to speak neither good nor bad. Alone at Peniel, Jacob wrestles till daybreak and is named Israel—'a prince with God.'
Jacob and Esau Reconciled / Dinah and Shechem
Esau runs to meet Jacob not with a sword but an embrace, and the brothers are reconciled. But at Shechem, Dinah is defiled, and her brothers avenge her with treacherous slaughter.
Return to Bethel; Deaths of Rachel and Isaac / Joseph's Dreams and the Coat of Many Colours / Joseph Sold into Egypt
God calls Jacob back to Bethel to worship; there Rachel dies bearing Benjamin, and Isaac is buried. Joseph, the beloved son, dreams of sheaves that bow, and his jealous brothers sell him into Egypt.
In a dark interlude, Judah's sons die for their wickedness, and he wrongs his widowed daughter-in-law Tamar. By her bold stratagem she secures the line through which Messiah would come.
Joseph and Potiphar's Wife / The Butler and the Baker
In Potiphar's house Joseph flees temptation but is falsely accused and cast into prison, yet the LORD is with him. There he interprets the dreams of Pharaoh's butler and baker.
When Pharaoh dreams of fat and lean kine, the forgotten Joseph is summoned to interpret. He is exalted over all Egypt to store against the coming famine, ruler second only to Pharaoh.
The Brothers' First Journey to Egypt / The Second Journey; Benjamin
Driven by famine, Joseph's brothers come to Egypt and bow before him unknowing. He tests them, demanding Benjamin, and their father Jacob yields the beloved son with trembling.
The Silver Cup; Judah's Plea / Joseph Reveals Himself
Joseph hides his cup in Benjamin's sack to prove his brothers' hearts, and Judah offers himself in the lad's stead. Then Joseph can restrain himself no longer and weeps: 'I am Joseph your brother.'
God speaks to Jacob in the night, and he goes down to Egypt with all his house. Joseph meets his father in Goshen, and the seventy souls of Israel are settled in the best of the land.
Joseph Administers the Famine / Jacob Blesses Ephraim and Manasseh
Through the famine Joseph gathers all Egypt's wealth for Pharaoh. Aged Jacob blesses Joseph's sons, crossing his hands to set the younger Ephraim above Manasseh.
Jacob Blesses His Sons; His Death / The Burial of Jacob; the Death of Joseph

Gathering his twelve sons, Jacob prophesies over each and yields up the ghost. His body is carried to Canaan for burial, and Joseph, forgiving his brothers, dies in Egypt with the promise on his lips: 'God will surely visit you.'
Israel Oppressed; the Hebrew Midwives / The Birth of Moses / Moses Flees to Midian
A new king who knew not Joseph enslaves Israel, and the midwives fear God rather than Pharaoh. Moses is drawn from the river and raised in the palace, then flees to Midian after slaying an Egyptian.
At the burning bush that is not consumed, God reveals His name, I AM THAT I AM, and commissions the reluctant Moses to deliver His people. Signs are given, and Aaron is appointed his mouth.
Moses returns to Egypt with the rod of God in his hand. He gathers the elders, shows the signs, and the people believe and bow their heads in worship.
Moses and Aaron demand that Pharaoh let Israel go, but he only increases their burden, commanding bricks without straw. The people murmur, yet God renews His covenant promise to redeem.
The Rod Becomes a Serpent / Plague 1: Water to Blood / Plague 2: Frogs / Plague 3: Lice / Plague 4: Flies
Aaron's rod becomes a serpent that swallows the sorcerers' rods. God unleashes the first plagues—blood, frogs, lice, and flies—and Pharaoh's heart is hardened against the outstretched hand of God.
Plague 5: Murrain on the Cattle / Plague 6: Boils / Plague 7: Hail
The plagues intensify upon Egypt: murrain slays the cattle, boils break out on man and beast, and hail smites the land. Yet God shelters Goshen, and Pharaoh will not relent.
Plague 8: Locusts / Plague 9: Darkness / The Final Plague Announced
Locusts devour what the hail left, and a darkness that may be felt covers Egypt three days. God announces the final and most terrible stroke: the death of the firstborn.
The Passover Instituted / Death of the Firstborn; the Exodus
God institutes the Passover: a lamb slain, its blood on the door, its flesh eaten in haste. At midnight the firstborn of Egypt die, and Israel goes out with a high hand.
The Pillar of Cloud and Fire / Crossing the Red Sea
God leads His people by a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night. Trapped at the sea, they see the LORD fight for them as the waters part, then close over Pharaoh's host.
The Song of Moses and Miriam / Bitter Water Made Sweet at Marah / Manna and Quail
Israel sings the song of triumph on the far shore. At Marah the bitter water is made sweet, and in the wilderness God rains down manna and quail, proving them whether they will walk in His law.
Water from the Rock; Victory over Amalek / Jethro's Counsel
When the people thirst and murmur, God brings water from the smitten rock, and Israel prevails over Amalek while Moses' hands are held up. Jethro counsels Moses to share the burden of judging.
Israel encamps before Sinai, and God descends in thunder, smoke, and trembling fire. He calls them to be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation unto Himself.
The Ten Commandments Given / The Covenant Confirmed; Moses on the Mount
From the mountain God speaks the Ten Commandments amid lightning and the trumpet's blast. The people pledge obedience, the covenant is sealed with blood, and Moses ascends into the glory-cloud.
The Golden Calf / Moses Intercedes; "Shew Me Thy Glory"
While Moses tarries, the people make a golden calf and corrupt themselves. Moses breaks the tables, intercedes for the guilty, and pleads, 'Shew me thy glory,' beholding the goodness of God.
The Tables Renewed; Moses' Shining Face
God renews the broken tables and passes before Moses, proclaiming His name merciful and gracious. Moses' face shines from speaking with God, and he veils it before the people.
The Tabernacle Built and Filled with Glory (Part 1)
The people bring their willing offerings, and the craftsmen begin the tabernacle just as God commanded. The curtains, boards, and coverings of the sanctuary take shape by wisdom given from above.
The Tabernacle Built and Filled with Glory (Part 2)
The holy furnishings are fashioned—the ark, the mercy seat, the table, the lampstand, and the altars—each after the pattern shown in the mount. The court is enclosed for the dwelling of God with men.
The Tabernacle Built and Filled with Glory (Part 3)
The priestly garments are made and the whole work is finished as the LORD commanded. Moses rears up the tabernacle, and the glory of the LORD fills it—God come down to dwell among His people.
The Sin of Nadab and Abihu / The Blasphemer Stoned
Nadab and Abihu offer strange fire before the LORD and are consumed, for God will be sanctified in them that draw near. So too the blasphemer is stoned, that His name be held holy.
Fire at Taberah; Quail and Plague at Kibroth-hattaavah
When the people complain, fire from the LORD burns at Taberah. Lusting for flesh, they are fed with quail until it comes out their nostrils, and plague strikes at Kibroth-hattaavah.
Miriam and Aaron Oppose Moses; Miriam's Leprosy / The Twelve Spies
Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses, and Miriam is struck leprous until Moses cries for her healing. Twelve spies search Canaan, but ten bring back an evil report of giants and walled cities.
Israel's Rebellion; Forty Years Decreed / The Sabbath-Breaker Stoned

Terrified by the spies, Israel weeps to return to Egypt, and God decrees forty years' wandering till that faithless generation falls. A man gathering sticks on the sabbath is stoned for despising the LORD's command.
Korah, Dathan, and Abiram rise against Moses and Aaron, and the earth opens to swallow them. Fire consumes the two hundred fifty, and God vindicates His chosen priesthood.
Aaron's Rod Buds / Water at Meribah; Moses' Sin / Edom Refuses Passage; the Death of Aaron

Aaron's rod alone buds, blossoms, and yields almonds as a sign against rebellion. At Meribah Moses smites the rock in anger and forfeits the promised land; Edom bars the way, and Aaron dies on Mount Hor.
The Brasen Serpent / Sihon and Og Defeated / Balaam and His Ass

When fiery serpents bite the murmuring people, God bids Moses lift up a brasen serpent, and all who look live. Sihon and Og are defeated, and Balak hires Balaam, whose own ass sees the angel he cannot.
Balak brings Balaam to curse Israel, but God turns the curse to blessing again and again. From the heights the prophet foretells a Star out of Jacob and a Sceptre that shall rise in Israel.
Baal-peor; the Zeal of Phinehas / The Daughters of Zelophehad / Joshua Appointed Successor

Seduced to Baal-peor, Israel plays the harlot until Phinehas' zeal turns away the plague. The daughters of Zelophehad receive their inheritance, and Joshua is set apart to lead when Moses is gathered.
At God's command Israel executes vengeance upon Midian for the sin of Peor. The spoil is divided, and a memorial offering is brought to the LORD.
Reuben and Gad Settle East of Jordan / Moses Pleads to Enter the Land
Reuben and Gad ask to settle east of Jordan and pledge to fight first for their brethren. Moses recounts how, for the people's sake, he was not suffered to cross over into the good land.
Moses Views the Land; the Death of Moses / Joshua Commissioned / Rahab and the Spies

From Nebo Moses views the land he may not enter, and dies at God's word, buried by His hand. Joshua is charged to be strong and of good courage, and Rahab hides the spies, hanging out her scarlet line of faith.
Crossing the Jordan; the Memorial Stones
The priests bearing the ark step into Jordan, and the waters stand up in a heap. All Israel passes over on dry ground, and twelve stones are raised at Gilgal as a memorial to their children.
Circumcision at Gilgal; the Captain of the LORD's Host / The Fall of Jericho
Israel is circumcised at Gilgal and keeps the Passover in the land, and the captain of the LORD's host appears with drawn sword. At the shout and the trumpet, Jericho's walls fall down flat.
Achan's Sin; Defeat at Ai / Ai Conquered / The Covenant Renewed at Mount Ebal
Achan's hidden sin brings defeat at Ai until it is judged and purged. Then Ai is taken by ambush, and Israel renews the covenant at Ebal and Gerizim, reading the blessing and the curse.
The Gibeonite Deception / The Sun Stands Still; the Southern Campaign

The Gibeonites deceive Joshua into a league by feigning a far journey. When five kings besiege them, God casts down great hailstones and the sun stands still upon Gibeon till Israel's foes are overthrown.
The Northern Campaign / Caleb Claims His Mountain
Joshua turns north and defeats the confederate kings at the waters of Merom. Caleb, at eighty-five, claims Hebron, saying, 'Give me this mountain,' his strength undimmed by faith.
The eastern tribes build a great altar by Jordan, and the others gather for war, fearing apostasy. But it proves an altar of witness, that their children might know they too belong to the LORD.

Joshua gathers Israel and rehearses God's faithfulness from Abraham until now. He sets before them the solemn choice—'choose you this day whom ye will serve'—vowing, 'as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.'
After Joshua's death the tribes go up to possess their lands but fail to drive out the Canaanites. Adoni-bezek reaps what he sowed, judged as he had judged others.
The Cycle of Apostasy Begins / Othniel / Ehud and Eglon / Shamgar
A generation arises that knew not the LORD, and the cycle of sin, servitude, and deliverance begins. God raises up judges—Othniel, Ehud who slays fat Eglon, and Shamgar—to save His people.
Deborah, Barak, and Jael / The Song of Deborah
Deborah the prophetess and Barak lead Israel against Sisera's iron chariots, and Jael drives a tent-peg through the sleeping captain's temple. Their song exalts the LORD who fights from heaven.
The Call of Gideon; the Fleece
When Midian oppresses Israel, the angel finds Gideon threshing in a winepress and calls him a mighty man of valour. Gideon lays out the fleece, and God answers, first wet, then dry.
Gideon's Three Hundred / Gideon's Pursuit; the Ephod
God pares Gideon's army to three hundred, that Israel might know the victory is His alone. With trumpets, pitchers, and torches they rout Midian, though Gideon's later ephod becomes a snare.
Abimelech and the Bramble King / Tola and Jair
Abimelech murders his brethren to make himself king, and Jotham's parable of the bramble foretells his ruin. He dies dishonoured by a woman's millstone, and quieter judges follow.
Israel again cries out under Ammon, and Jephthah the outcast is called to lead. He conquers, but his rash vow costs him his only daughter.
Shibboleth / Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon / The Birth of Samson
Ephraim's men cannot say 'Shibboleth' and fall at the fords of Jordan. Minor judges arise, and the angel announces to barren Manoah's wife the birth of Samson, a Nazarite from the womb.
Samson's Riddle and Marriage / The Foxes and the Jawbone
Samson poses a riddle at his wedding feast and is betrayed by his bride. In fury he burns the Philistines' fields and, with the jawbone of an ass, slays a thousand men.
Samson and Delilah; His Death / Micah's Idols

Delilah wears down Samson until he yields the secret of his strength, and shorn and blinded he grinds in prison. In death he pulls down the temple of Dagon upon his foes. Meanwhile Micah sets up idols in his house.
The Danites Steal Micah's Gods / The Levite's Concubine
The Danites steal Micah's graven gods and priest as they seek an inheritance. In the darkest chapter, a Levite's concubine is abused to death at Gibeah, and Israel is roused to horror.
War Against Benjamin / Wives for Benjamin

Israel goes to war against Benjamin for the outrage at Gibeah, and the tribe is all but destroyed. To preserve it, wives are found for the survivors—for in those days there was no king, and every man did what was right in his own eyes.
Naomi and Ruth Return to Bethlehem / Ruth Gleans in the Field of Boaz
Bereft of husband and sons, Naomi returns to Bethlehem, and Ruth the Moabitess cleaves to her: 'thy God shall be my God.' Ruth gleans in the field of Boaz, a near kinsman, and finds favour.
Ruth at the Threshing Floor / Boaz Redeems Ruth

At Naomi's counsel Ruth lies at Boaz's feet and claims the kinsman's care. Boaz redeems her and the inheritance, and their son Obed becomes grandfather to David—grace grafting a stranger into the line of Christ.
Hannah's Prayer; the Birth of Samuel / Hannah's Song; the Sons of Eli

Barren Hannah pours out her soul at Shiloh, vowing her son to the LORD, and God grants her Samuel. Her song magnifies the God who raises the poor from the dust while Eli's wicked sons profane the offering.
God Calls Samuel / The Ark Captured; Ichabod
The LORD calls the child Samuel in the night, and he answers, 'Speak, for thy servant heareth.' Israel is defeated and the ark captured; Eli falls dead, and Ichabod is named—'the glory is departed.'
Dagon Falls Before the Ark / The Ark Returned
The captured ark topples Dagon in his own temple and afflicts the Philistines with plagues. Fearing the God of Israel, they send it back on a new cart with a trespass offering.
Ebenezer: "Hitherto Hath the LORD Helped Us" / Israel Demands a King
Samuel calls Israel to repent, and God thunders against the Philistines; he sets up Ebenezer, 'hitherto hath the LORD helped us.' But the people, rejecting God's rule, demand a king like the nations.
Seeking his father's lost asses, Saul is led to Samuel, who anoints him captain over Israel. God gives him another heart, and he is chosen by lot before all the people.
Saul Delivers Jabesh-gilead / Samuel's Farewell Address
Saul's spirit is stirred to rescue Jabesh-gilead, and the kingdom is confirmed at Gilgal. Samuel gives his farewell, testifying to his own integrity and warning Israel to fear the LORD.
Saul's Unlawful Sacrifice / Jonathan's Daring Raid; Saul's Rash Oath
Impatient at Gilgal, Saul offers the sacrifice himself and is told his kingdom shall not continue. Jonathan's faith routs the Philistines, but Saul's rash oath nearly costs his son his life.
Saul Rejected; "To Obey Is Better Than Sacrifice" / David Anointed; David Plays for Saul
For sparing Agag and the spoil, Saul is rejected: 'to obey is better than sacrifice.' Samuel anoints the shepherd boy David, and the Spirit departs from Saul, who is soothed by David's harp.
The giant Goliath defies the armies of the living God, but the shepherd David comes in the name of the LORD. With a sling and a stone he fells the champion, for the battle is the LORD's.
Jonathan's Covenant; Saul's Jealousy / Michal Helps David Escape
Jonathan's soul is knit to David's in covenant love, but Saul's jealousy festers into murderous rage. Twice the king hurls his javelin, and Michal lets David down through a window to escape.
Jonathan tests his father's heart and, with arrows shot beyond the lad, warns David to flee. The two friends weep and part, bound by an oath before the LORD forever.
The Shewbread; David Feigns Madness at Gath / The Cave of Adullam; the Priests of Nob Slain
Fleeing, David eats the holy shewbread at Nob and feigns madness before the king of Gath. He gathers a band at Adullam, while Saul in fury slaughters the priests who unwittingly aided him.
David Saves Keilah; Hunted in Ziph / David Spares Saul in the Cave

David delivers Keilah yet is hunted through the wilderness of Ziph, preserved by God's hand. In the cave he cuts Saul's robe but spares the LORD's anointed, refusing to lift his hand against the king.
Churlish Nabal insults David, who sets out to avenge himself, until wise Abigail meets him with gifts and counsel. She stays his hand from bloodshed, and when Nabal dies, she becomes David's wife.
David Spares Saul Again: the Spear and the Cruse / David at Ziklag Among the Philistines
By night David takes Saul's spear and cruse but again spares his life, calling across the valley. Weary of the pursuit, David takes refuge among the Philistines at Ziklag.
Saul and the Witch of Endor / The Philistines Dismiss David
Forsaken by God, Saul seeks the witch of Endor, and Samuel's shade foretells his doom. Meanwhile the Philistine lords distrust David and send him back from the coming battle.

Returning to find Ziklag burned and their families taken, David's men speak of stoning him, but he encourages himself in the LORD. He pursues the raiders and recovers all, sharing the spoil alike with all his men.
The Death of Saul and Jonathan / David Hears of Saul's Death; the Lament
On Gilboa, Saul and his sons fall before the Philistines, and the king takes his own life. When word reaches David, he does not rejoice but rends his clothes and laments 'how are the mighty fallen.'
David King over Judah; Civil War Begins / Abner Defects and Is Murdered

David is anointed king over Judah at Hebron while Ish-bosheth reigns over the north, and long war divides the house. Abner turns to David but is treacherously murdered by Joab, whom David publicly mourns.
Ish-bosheth Murdered / David King over All Israel; Jerusalem Taken
Ish-bosheth is slain by his own captains, whom David judges for their treachery. Then all Israel comes to Hebron, and David, thirty years old, takes the stronghold of Zion for his throne.
The Ark Brought to Jerusalem; Uzzah; Michal / The Davidic Covenant
Bringing up the ark, Uzzah is struck for touching it, and David dances before the LORD while Michal despises him. God covenants that David's house and throne shall be established forever.

David subdues his enemies on every side, and the LORD preserves him whithersoever he goes. Remembering his covenant with Jonathan, he shows kindness to lame Mephibosheth and sets him at the king's table.
War with Ammon and Syria / David and Bath-sheba
While Israel wars with Ammon and Syria, David tarries at Jerusalem and falls. He takes Bath-sheba and, to hide his sin, has faithful Uriah slain in the forefront of the battle.
Nathan's Parable: "Thou Art the Man" / Amnon and Tamar; Absalom's Revenge
Nathan's parable of the ewe lamb pierces the king's heart—'thou art the man'—and David repents, though the sword will not depart from his house. Amnon defiles Tamar, and Absalom nurses vengeance.
The Woman of Tekoah; Absalom Recalled / Absalom's Rebellion; David Flees
By the wise woman of Tekoah, Joab wins Absalom's recall, though the king's heart is not fully turned. Absalom steals the hearts of Israel and raises rebellion, and David flees weeping over Olivet.
Ziba's Deceit; Shimei Curses David / Ahithophel and Hushai
Ziba slanders Mephibosheth, and Shimei curses the fleeing king, who bears it as from the LORD. Ahithophel's shrewd counsel is overthrown by Hushai's, God working to save David.
The Death of Absalom / David's Return; Mephibosheth and Barzillai
Absalom is caught by his hair in an oak and slain by Joab against the king's command. David's cry, 'O my son Absalom,' turns victory to mourning, until he is recalled to reign in peace.
The Revolt of Sheba / The Gibeonites Avenged; Battles with the Giants
Sheba blows the trumpet of revolt but perishes when a wise woman casts his head over the wall. The Gibeonites are avenged, and David's mighty men slay the last of the giants of Gath.
David's Mighty Men / David's Census; the Plague; Araunah's Threshing Floor

The roll of David's mighty men records their valiant deeds. But David numbers the people in pride, and the plague falls until he builds an altar on Araunah's threshing floor, refusing to offer that which costs him nothing.
As David lies dying, Adonijah exalts himself to be king. Nathan and Bath-sheba move quickly, and Solomon is anointed at Gihon amid the people's shout, 'God save king Solomon.'
David's Charge; Solomon's Throne Established / Solomon Asks for Wisdom; the Two Mothers

David charges Solomon to keep the ways of the LORD, and the kingdom is established in his hand. At Gibeon God offers Solomon his heart's desire, and he asks for an understanding heart, discerned soon in the judgment of the two mothers.
In league with Hiram of Tyre, Solomon gathers cedar and stone and begins the house of the LORD. The temple rises in silence, without hammer or axe heard, a dwelling for the God of Israel.

Solomon completes the temple's furnishings—the pillars Jachin and Boaz, the molten sea, the lavers, and the vessels of gold—all the work of Hiram the craftsman. His own palace and its courts are also built.
The Temple Dedicated; Glory Fills the House

The ark is brought into the holy of holies, and the glory-cloud fills the house so the priests cannot stand. Solomon blesses the people and prays that God would hear from heaven all who turn toward this place.
God Appears to Solomon the Second Time / The Queen of Sheba

God appears again to Solomon, promising blessing for obedience and warning of exile for apostasy. The queen of Sheba comes to prove him with hard questions and finds the half was not told her of his wisdom and glory.
Solomon's many foreign wives turn his heart after other gods, and the LORD is angry. Adversaries are raised up, and the seeds of the kingdom's division are sown in his old age.
The Kingdom Divided; Jeroboam's Golden Calves / The Man of God from Judah and the Old Prophet

When Rehoboam threatens heavier burdens, ten tribes tear away under Jeroboam, who sets up golden calves at Dan and Bethel. A man of God cries against the altar but is slain for disobeying the LORD's own word.
Ahijah's Prophecy; the Death of Jeroboam's Son / Elijah, the Ravens, and the Widow of Zarephath
Ahijah foretells doom on Jeroboam's house, and his son dies. In famine, Elijah is fed by ravens and by the widow of Zarephath, whose meal and oil do not fail and whose dead son is raised.
On Carmel Elijah confronts the prophets of Baal—'how long halt ye between two opinions?' Fire falls from heaven to consume the sacrifice, and the people cry, 'The LORD, he is the God.'
Elijah Flees; the Still Small Voice; Elisha Called / Ahab Defeats Ben-hadad
Fleeing Jezebel, Elijah despairs under the juniper, and God comes not in wind or fire but in a still small voice. Elisha is called to follow, and Ahab, against odds, defeats Ben-hadad of Syria.
Naboth's Vineyard / Micaiah's Prophecy; the Death of Ahab

Jezebel murders Naboth to seize his vineyard, and Elijah pronounces judgment on Ahab's house. Micaiah alone foretells the truth of Ramoth-gilead, and a random arrow finds the disguised king, fulfilling the word of the LORD.
Fire from Heaven on Ahaziah's Captains / Elijah Taken Up; Elisha Takes the Mantle / The Waters Healed; the Mocking Youths

Ahaziah's captains are consumed by fire from heaven for their arrogance toward the prophet. Elijah is carried up in a whirlwind, and Elisha takes up the fallen mantle to heal the waters and see judgment fall.
Moab Rebels; Water Fills the Valley / The Widow's Oil / The Shunammite's Son Raised / Death in the Pot; a Hundred Men Fed

Water fills the valley without wind or rain, and the widow's oil overflows every borrowed vessel. Elisha raises the Shunammite's son, purges the deadly pottage, and feeds a hundred men with twenty loaves.
Naaman Healed; Gehazi's Leprosy / The Axe Head Floats / Chariots of Fire; the Syrians Blinded

Naaman the leper is cleansed by dipping seven times in Jordan, while greedy Gehazi inherits his leprosy. The axe head swims at the prophet's word, and horses and chariots of fire encircle the mountain.
The Siege of Samaria; the Four Lepers
Besieged Samaria starves until Elisha foretells sudden plenty. Four lepers stumble into the deserted Syrian camp, and the deliverance of the LORD comes overnight as the prophet said.
The Shunammite's Land Restored; Hazael / Jehu Anointed; the Deaths of Joram and Jezebel
The Shunammite's land is restored, and Hazael's cruelty is foretold with tears. Jehu is anointed to execute judgment, and Joram and painted Jezebel meet the deaths the LORD decreed.
Jehu Destroys the House of Ahab and Baal Worship
Jehu roots out the whole house of Ahab and gathers the worshippers of Baal to destroy them. He purges Baal from Israel, yet does not depart from the golden calves of Jeroboam.
Athaliah's Usurpation; Joash Hidden and Crowned / Joash Repairs the Temple
Wicked Athaliah destroys the royal seed, but infant Joash is hidden in the temple six years. Jehoiada crowns the boy king and slays the usurper, and Joash later repairs the house of the LORD.
The Death of Elisha; His Bones Revive a Man
The dying Elisha gives Joash a final sign of victory over Syria. So great was the prophet's God that a corpse cast into Elisha's grave revives at the touch of his bones.
Amaziah Challenges Jehoash: the Thistle and the Cedar / Ahaz Copies the Altar of Damascus
Amaziah, puffed up, challenges Jehoash, who answers with the parable of the thistle and the cedar, and Judah is humbled. Ahaz copies a heathen altar from Damascus, forsaking the LORD.
For its persistent idolatry the northern kingdom falls to Assyria and is carried away. The land is resettled with strangers who fear the LORD and serve their own gods together.

Assyria sweeps through Judah, and Rabshakeh blasphemes the living God before Jerusalem's walls. Hezekiah spreads the letter before the LORD, and the angel smites a hundred fourscore and five thousand in the night.
Hezekiah's Illness; the Shadow Turns Back
Sick unto death, Hezekiah turns his face to the wall and prays, and God adds fifteen years to his life. As a sign, the shadow goes back ten degrees on the dial of Ahaz.
The Wickedness of Manasseh / Josiah Finds the Book of the Law
Manasseh fills Jerusalem with blood and idolatry, the worst of Judah's kings. Long after, young Josiah repairs the temple, where the lost book of the law is found and read with trembling.

Josiah reads the covenant to all the people and sweeps away the idols, altars, and high places. He keeps a Passover unequalled since the judges, yet falls at Megiddo, and Judah's reprieve ends with him.
The Fall of Jerusalem; Judah Carried Captive
Babylon comes up against Jerusalem, and after siege and famine the city and temple are burned. Zedekiah's sons are slain before his blinded eyes, and Judah is carried captive to Babylon.
The Prayer of Jabez / David Prepares Materials for the Temple

Amid the genealogies, Jabez cries to God to bless him and enlarge his coast, and God grants his request. David, forbidden to build, gathers abundant materials and charges Solomon to build the house of the LORD.
David's Charge to Solomon; the Freewill Offering

Before the assembly David charges Solomon to serve God with a perfect heart and a willing mind. The princes and people offer willingly for the temple, and David blesses the LORD, 'thine is the kingdom.'
Abijah's Victory over Jeroboam / Asa's Victory over Zerah the Ethiopian
Abijah trusts the LORD against Jeroboam's greater host and prevails, for Judah relies on God. Asa cries to the LORD against a million Ethiopians, and the innumerable army is overthrown before him.

Threatened by a great multitude, Jehoshaphat sets himself to seek the LORD and proclaims a fast. Judah goes out singing praise, and God sets ambushes so their enemies destroy one another—'the battle is not yours, but God's.'
Uzziah's Pride and Leprosy / Hezekiah's Great Passover

Uzziah prospers until pride leads him to burn incense unlawfully, and he is struck leprous to his death. Hezekiah cleanses the temple and keeps a great Passover, inviting even the remnant of the north to return.

Manasseh is bound and carried to Babylon, where in affliction he humbles himself greatly before God. The LORD is entreated, restores him to his throne, and Manasseh comes at last to know that the LORD is God.
The Decree of Cyrus; the Return
The LORD stirs the spirit of Cyrus to proclaim liberty for the captives to rebuild the house of God. A remnant returns to Jerusalem, their names and offerings recorded, to begin the work.
The Altar Rebuilt; the Foundation Laid / Opposition Halts the Work
The returned exiles build the altar and keep the feasts, then lay the temple's foundation with weeping and shouting. But the adversaries of Judah hire counsellors and by intrigue halt the work.
The Work Resumes; Darius Confirms the Decree
Stirred by Haggai and Zechariah, the people resume building, and Darius searches the archives. Finding Cyrus's decree, the king confirms it and funds the work, and the house is finished with joy.

Ezra the ready scribe comes up from Babylon with a company, his hand strengthened by his God. Ashamed to ask a guard, he proclaims a fast, entrusting the journey and the treasure to the LORD's protecting hand.

Ezra is grieved to find the people joined in marriage to the heathen, and he rends his garment and confesses their guilt. The congregation covenants to put away the strange wives and turn back to the LORD.
Nehemiah Weeps and Prays for Jerusalem / Before the King; the Night Inspection
Hearing of Jerusalem's ruin, Nehemiah weeps, fasts, and prays for many days. Before Artaxerxes his sad countenance opens the way, and by night he surveys the broken walls, resolved to build.

The people set their hands to build, each over against his own house. When Sanballat and Tobiah mock and conspire, Nehemiah sets a watch, so that with one hand they wrought and with the other held a weapon.
Nehemiah Stops the Oppression of the Poor
Nehemiah confronts the nobles for enslaving their own brethren with usury in the famine. Moved by his rebuke, they restore the lands and the debts, and he asks nothing for himself.
Plots Against Nehemiah; the Wall Finished in 52 Days / Ezra Reads the Law; the Feast of Tabernacles

Enemies scheme to frighten Nehemiah from the work, but he will not come down, and the wall is finished in fifty-two days. Ezra reads the law from morning till midday, and the people weep, then keep the feast with joy.
Gathered in sackcloth, the people hear the record of God's mercies and their fathers' rebellions. They make a sure covenant, sealed by their princes, to walk in the law of God.
With thanksgiving and singing the wall is dedicated, two great companies going round about upon it. The joy of Jerusalem is heard afar off.

Nehemiah returns to purge the temple, the sabbath, and the mixed marriages once more, praying, 'Remember me, O my God, for good.' Far off in Persia, proud Vashti is deposed for refusing the king's command.
Esther Made Queen; Mordecai Uncovers a Plot / Haman's Decree Against the Jews
Esther the Jewess is chosen queen, and Mordecai uncovers a plot against the king's life. But Haman, enraged that Mordecai will not bow, buys a decree to destroy all the Jews in a single day.
"For Such a Time as This" / Esther's First Banquet; Haman's Gallows

Mordecai charges Esther that she is come to the kingdom 'for such a time as this.' Risking death, she approaches the king and invites him and Haman to a banquet, while Haman builds a gallows for Mordecai.
The King Honours Mordecai / Haman Hanged on His Own Gallows

Unable to sleep, the king reads how Mordecai once saved him and commands Haman to honour his enemy through the streets. At the second banquet Esther unmasks the plot, and Haman is hanged on his own gallows.
The New Decree; the Jews Delivered; Purim
A new decree lets the Jews defend themselves, and their sorrow is turned into deliverance. The feast of Purim is established to remember how God preserved His people from destruction.
Job's Testing: Satan Before the LORD
Satan appears before the LORD and receives leave to strike upright Job. In one day Job loses his children, his wealth, and his health, yet he sins not: 'the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away.'
God Answers out of the Whirlwind; Job Restored (Part 1)
Out of the whirlwind God answers Job with questions of creation—'where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?' The wonders of sea and sky and beast declare a wisdom beyond man's reach.
God Answers out of the Whirlwind; Job Restored (Part 2)
God challenges Job to array himself with majesty if he would contend, showing behemoth and leviathan whom none can tame. The greatness of the Creator silences every complaint.
God Answers out of the Whirlwind; Job Restored (Part 3)
Job repents in dust and ashes, having seen God with his eyes, and prays for his friends. The LORD turns his captivity and blesses his latter end more than his beginning.
Isaiah's Vision and Call: "Here Am I; Send Me" / Isaiah's Three-Year Sign: Naked and Barefoot
Isaiah sees the LORD high and lifted up, is cleansed by a coal from the altar, and answers, 'Here am I; send me.' As a living sign he walks stripped and barefoot, warning Egypt's trust will fail.

Assyria's Rabshakeh reviles the LORD before Jerusalem, and Hezekiah spreads the threatening letter before God. Isaiah promises deliverance, and the angel of the LORD smites the Assyrian host in the night.

Hezekiah is healed and given a sign as the sun's shadow returns backward. But when Babylon's envoys come, he displays his treasures in pride, and Isaiah foretells that all will one day be carried to Babylon.
The Call of Jeremiah / Jeremiah's Linen Girdle
Before he was formed, God ordained Jeremiah a prophet to the nations and touched his mouth. The marred linen girdle becomes a sign of a proud people who cling to God no longer.
At the Potter's House / The Broken Bottle in the Valley of Hinnom
At the potter's house Jeremiah learns that God shapes and reshapes the nations as clay in His hand. He breaks a bottle in Hinnom to signify a judgment on Jerusalem that cannot be mended.
Jeremiah's Trial After the Temple Sermon / Hananiah Breaks the Yoke
For preaching the temple's doom Jeremiah is seized and nearly slain, but spared by the elders. Hananiah breaks the prophet's wooden yoke with a false promise of peace, and dies for his lie.
Jeremiah Buys the Field at Anathoth
As the Babylonians besiege the city, Jeremiah buys a field at Anathoth by God's command. The deed, sealed and preserved, is a pledge that houses and fields shall be bought again in the land.
The Obedience of the Rechabites / Jehoiakim Burns the Scroll
The Rechabites refuse wine in faithfulness to their father's charge, shaming a disobedient nation. When Jehoiakim cuts and burns Jeremiah's scroll, God commands it written again, with judgment added.
Jeremiah in the Dungeon; Ebed-melech's Rescue
Jeremiah is cast into a miry dungeon to silence his warning, sinking in the mire. Ebed-melech the Ethiopian pleads for him and draws him up with cords and old rags, and God remembers his kindness.
The Fall of Jerusalem; Gedaliah; Flight to Egypt (Part 1)
Jerusalem falls; Zedekiah is captured, and Jeremiah is freed and left in the land. Gedaliah is set as governor, and Jeremiah dwells among the remnant of the poor.
The Fall of Jerusalem; Gedaliah; Flight to Egypt (Part 2)
Gedaliah is treacherously murdered, and the frightened remnant asks Jeremiah to seek God's will. Though warned to stay, they resolve to flee to Egypt.
The Fall of Jerusalem; Gedaliah; Flight to Egypt (Part 3)
Against the word of the LORD the remnant carries Jeremiah down into Egypt. There the prophet foretells that Babylon's judgment will reach them even in their refuge.
Ezekiel's Vision of the Wheels; His Call (Part 1)
By the river Chebar Ezekiel sees the whirlwind, the living creatures, the wheels within wheels, and the likeness of the glory of God. He falls upon his face before the throne above the firmament.
Ezekiel's Vision of the Wheels; His Call (Part 2)
God makes Ezekiel a watchman to the house of Israel and warns that their blood is on his hands if he keeps silent. The prophet eats the scroll sweet as honey and is sent to a rebellious people.
Ezekiel's Sign-Acts: the Tile, the Siege, and the Baggage (Part 1)

Ezekiel portrays the siege of Jerusalem upon a tile and lies bound on his side to bear their years of iniquity. By shaven hair divided and scattered he signifies the coming sword, famine, and dispersion.
Ezekiel's Sign-Acts: the Tile, the Siege, and the Baggage (Part 2)
Ezekiel digs through the wall and carries out his baggage by night, a sign of the exile of the prince and people. His trembling bread and water show the dismay of a city about to be taken.
The Temple Vision: Idolatry Within; the Glory Departs (Part 1)
In vision Ezekiel is carried to the temple and shown the hidden abominations of the elders. The man with the inkhorn marks the mourners for mercy before the slaughter begins.
The Temple Vision: Idolatry Within; the Glory Departs (Part 2)
The cherubim and wheels move as the glory of the LORD rises from the threshold. Slowly the glory departs from the temple and the city, for God will not dwell where He is despised.
The Death of Ezekiel's Wife: a Sign to Israel / The Valley of Dry Bones

Ezekiel's wife, the desire of his eyes, is taken, and he is forbidden to mourn—a sign of the fall of the sanctuary. In the valley of dry bones the breath of God enters the slain, and a whole army lives, a promise of resurrection for Israel.
Ezekiel prophesies against Gog of the land of Magog, who comes up against God's regathered people. The LORD Himself overthrows the invader, that the nations may know He is holy.
God bids Hosea take Gomer, a wife of whoredoms, whose wandering pictures Israel's unfaithfulness. Their children bear names of judgment, yet God promises to say again, 'Thou art my people.'
Hosea buys back his adulterous wife and loves her still, as the LORD loves faithless Israel. So Israel shall abide many days and afterward return and seek the LORD their God.
Amaziah the priest of Bethel accuses the herdsman Amos and bids him flee to Judah. Amos answers that the LORD took him from the flock and sent him to prophesy against Israel.
The Five Visions of Amos: Locusts, Fire, Plumbline, Summer Fruit, the Altar (Part 1)
The LORD shows Amos locusts and fire, and at the prophet's plea relents; then the plumbline measures Israel's crookedness. The basket of summer fruit declares the end is come upon His people.
The Five Visions of Amos: Locusts, Fire, Plumbline, Summer Fruit, the Altar (Part 2)

Amos sees the LORD standing upon the altar, and none shall escape His hand of judgment. Yet the vision closes with hope: God will raise up the fallen tabernacle of David and restore His people to their land.
By night Zechariah sees the man among the myrtle trees, the horns and carpenters, and the man with the measuring line. God declares His jealousy for Zion and His purpose to dwell in her midst.

Joshua the high priest, clothed in filth, is given clean garments—a picture of the Branch who removes iniquity. The golden candlestick and two olive trees teach that it is 'not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.'

The flying roll and the woman in the ephah carry away wickedness to its own place. The four chariots go forth, and crowns are set on Joshua's head, foreshadowing the Branch who is priest upon His throne.
Daniel Refuses the King's Meat / Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Great Image

Daniel and his friends refuse the king's defiling meat and are found fairer and wiser than all. When none can tell the king's forgotten dream, God reveals it to Daniel: a great image and a stone that fills the earth.
The Fiery Furnace / Nebuchadnezzar's Madness and Restoration

The three Hebrews refuse to bow and are cast into the furnace, where a fourth walks with them unharmed. Proud Nebuchadnezzar is driven to eat grass like an ox until he learns that the Most High rules.
Belshazzar's Feast; the Handwriting on the Wall
At Belshazzar's feast the sacred vessels are profaned, and a hand writes upon the wall. Daniel reads the doom—'weighed in the balances, and found wanting'—and that night the king is slain.
Daniel in the Lions' Den / The Vision of the Four Beasts
For praying to his God, Daniel is cast to the lions, but an angel shuts their mouths. In vision he sees four beasts and the Ancient of days, and one like the Son of man given an everlasting kingdom.
The Ram and the He Goat / Daniel's Prayer; the Seventy Weeks

The ram and the he goat foretell the rise and fall of empires. As Daniel prays and confesses his people's sin, Gabriel comes with the prophecy of the seventy weeks that mark the coming of Messiah the Prince.
The Vision by the River Hiddekel; the Final Prophecy (Part 1)
By the river Hiddekel Daniel is strengthened by a glorious messenger and shown things to come. Kings of the north and south rise and fall in long conflict, all under the hand of God.
The Vision by the River Hiddekel; the Final Prophecy (Part 2)

Michael stands up for God's people in a time of trouble such as never was, and many that sleep in the dust shall awake. Daniel is told to seal the words and rest, for he shall stand in his lot at the end of the days.
Fleeing God's call to Nineveh, Jonah is cast into the sea and swallowed by a great fish. From the fish's belly he prays, and salvation is of the LORD.
Nineveh Repents; Jonah and the Gourd

Nineveh hears Jonah's cry and repents in sackcloth from the greatest to the least, and God spares the city. Angry that mercy was shown, Jonah is rebuked by the withered gourd: shall not God pity a great city?
Gabriel Announces John's Birth to Zacharias / The Annunciation to Mary / Mary Visits Elisabeth; the Magnificat / The Birth of John the Baptist / The Angel Appears to Joseph
Gabriel promises a son to aged Zacharias and announces to the virgin Mary that she shall bear the Son of God. Mary magnifies the Lord, John is born, and an angel bids Joseph take Mary as his wife.
The Birth of Jesus / The Shepherds and the Angels / Simeon and Anna in the Temple / The Visit of the Wise Men / The Flight to Egypt; the Slaughter of the Innocents

In Bethlehem the Word is made flesh; angels proclaim glad tidings and shepherds hasten to the manger. Simeon and Anna bless the child, wise men bring gifts, and the holy family flees Herod's sword into Egypt.
The Boy Jesus in the Temple
At twelve, Jesus is left behind in Jerusalem and found in the temple among the teachers. 'Wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?' Yet He returns and is subject to His parents.
The Ministry of John the Baptist (Part 1)
John the Baptist preaches in the wilderness, 'Repent ye, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand,' and baptizes in Jordan. He is the voice crying, preparing the way of the LORD.
The Ministry of John the Baptist (Part 2)
John warns the multitudes to bring forth fruits of repentance and points beyond himself. 'Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world'—he must decrease that Christ may increase.

Jesus comes to be baptized, and John, protesting his unworthiness, yields to fulfil all righteousness. The heavens open, the Spirit descends as a dove, and the Father's voice declares, 'This is my beloved Son.'
The Spirit that descended now leads Jesus into the wilderness. The full account tells how the Anointed enters His public ministry under heaven's approval.
Led into the wilderness, Jesus fasts forty days and is tempted by Satan. To every assault He answers, 'It is written,' overcoming by the word of God.
The tempter offers bread, spectacle, and the kingdoms of the world, but Christ will worship God alone. Defeated, the devil departs for a season, and angels come and minister to Him.
The First Disciples: Andrew, Peter, Philip, Nathanael
John's testimony draws Andrew, who finds his brother Simon; Jesus names him Cephas. Philip is called, and Nathanael confesses, 'Thou art the Son of God; thou art the King of Israel.'
Water to Wine at Cana / The First Cleansing of the Temple / Nicodemus: "Ye Must Be Born Again"
At Cana Jesus turns water into wine, manifesting His glory. He cleanses the temple with a scourge, and by night tells Nicodemus, 'Ye must be born again,' for God so loved the world.
The Woman at the Well / The Nobleman's Son Healed / Rejection at Nazareth
At Jacob's well Jesus offers a Samaritan woman living water and reveals Himself as Messiah. He heals the nobleman's son by a word, but at Nazareth His own would cast Him from the brow of the hill.
After a fruitless night, Peter lets down the net at Jesus' word and takes a great multitude of fishes. Astonished, he falls at Jesus' knees, and is called henceforth to catch men.
The call by the sea gathers the fishermen to leave all and follow. They forsake their nets to become the first companions of the Lord.
In the synagogue at Capernaum an unclean spirit cries out, and Jesus rebukes it with authority. The man is delivered, and His fame spreads abroad throughout Galilee.
At Peter's house Jesus heals his wife's mother of a fever, and she rises to serve. At evening the whole city gathers, and He heals their sick and casts out the spirits.
The full account shows Him healing many and departing to solitary places to pray. He must preach the kingdom to other cities also, for therefore is He sent.

A leper worships, saying, 'Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean,' and Jesus, moved with compassion, touches him: 'I will; be thou clean.' The man is healed and bidden to show himself to the priest.
So great is the fame of the cleansing that multitudes press to hear and be healed. Yet Jesus withdraws into the wilderness to pray.
The Paralytic Let Down Through the Roof (Part 1)
Four men bear a palsied man and, unable to enter for the press, let him down through the roof. Jesus forgives his sins and, to prove His authority, bids him take up his bed and walk.
The Paralytic Let Down Through the Roof (Part 2)
The people are amazed and glorify God, saying they have seen strange things. The power of the Lord is present to heal.
Passing by, Jesus calls Matthew the publican from the receipt of custom, and he leaves all to follow. At the feast with sinners He answers the murmurers: 'They that be whole need not a physician.'
When questioned about fasting, Jesus speaks of the bridegroom, and of new wine in new bottles. His coming makes all things new.
The Impotent Man at the Pool of Bethesda

At Bethesda's pool Jesus heals a man impotent thirty-eight years, bidding him rise and walk. Because it was the sabbath, the rulers seek to slay Him, but He answers, 'My Father worketh hitherto, and I work.'
Lord of the Sabbath: the Corn Fields and the Withered Hand (Part 1)
When the disciples pluck corn on the sabbath, Jesus declares the Son of man Lord even of the sabbath. He asks whether it is lawful to do good on the sabbath day.
Lord of the Sabbath: the Corn Fields and the Withered Hand (Part 2)
In the synagogue He heals the man with the withered hand, though the Pharisees watch to accuse Him. Grieved at their hardness, He does good, and they take counsel to destroy Him.
After a night of prayer in the mountain, Jesus chooses twelve to be with Him and to be sent forth. From all His followers He names the apostles who will bear His word.

On the mountain Jesus opens His mouth and blesses the poor in spirit, the meek, and the pure in heart. He teaches the higher righteousness of the kingdom—of anger, lust, love of enemies, and secret prayer.
The sermon continues: judge not, ask and it shall be given, enter by the strait gate. The wise man builds upon the rock of hearing and doing, and the people are astonished at His authority.
A centurion pleads for his servant, saying, 'Speak the word only.' Jesus marvels at faith not found in Israel, and heals the servant in that selfsame hour.
The Widow of Nain's Son Raised
At the gate of Nain Jesus meets a widow following her only son to burial. Moved with compassion, He touches the bier and says, 'Young man, arise,' and restores him to his mother.
John the Baptist's Question from Prison
John sends from prison to ask, 'Art thou he that should come?' Jesus points to the blind seeing and the poor hearing the gospel. Then He praises John as more than a prophet.
A woman known as a sinner washes Jesus' feet with tears and wipes them with her hair. To the scornful host He says, 'Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much.'

When Jesus casts out a devil, the Pharisees blaspheme that He does it by Beelzebub. He warns that a house divided cannot stand, and speaks of the sin against the Holy Ghost that shall not be forgiven.
The Parables by the Sea (the Sower and Others) (Part 1)
By the sea Jesus teaches in parables: the sower and the soils, the tares, the mustard seed, and the leaven. To His own He explains that the seed is the word, and the harvest is the end of the age.
The Parables by the Sea (the Sower and Others) (Part 2)
The parables reveal the mysteries of the kingdom to those with ears to hear. A candle is not hid, and what is sown in the heart will be made manifest.

As they cross the lake a great storm arises, and Jesus sleeps in the hinder part of the ship. Awakened, He rebukes the wind and sea—'Peace, be still'—and the disciples marvel, 'What manner of man is this?'
The full account shows the sudden calm and the disciples' fear turned to wonder. Even the winds and water obey Him.
Among the tombs a man possessed by a legion of devils meets Jesus, who sends the spirits into the swine. The herd runs violently into the sea, and the man is found clothed and in his right mind.
The delivered man begs to follow, but Jesus sends him to publish how great things God has done for him. The frightened people beseech Jesus to depart from their coasts.
Jairus's Daughter; the Woman with the Issue of Blood (Part 1)
Jairus falls at Jesus' feet for his dying daughter, and on the way a woman with an issue of blood touches His hem and is made whole. 'Thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace.'
Jairus's Daughter; the Woman with the Issue of Blood (Part 2)
Told the maid is dead, Jesus says, 'Fear not: believe only.' He takes her by the hand, 'Talitha cumi—Damsel, arise,' and life returns to her.
Two Blind Men and a Dumb Demoniac Healed
Two blind men follow crying for mercy, and Jesus touches their eyes: 'According to your faith be it unto you.' A dumb man possessed is delivered and speaks, and the multitudes marvel.

Jesus sends the twelve with power over unclean spirits, charging them to preach the kingdom freely. They are warned of persecution but promised the Father's care, for the very hairs of their head are numbered.
The apostles go through the towns preaching the gospel and healing everywhere. They return to tell Jesus all that they had done.
The Death of John the Baptist
Herod, snared by his oath at Herodias's daughter's dance, beheads John the Baptist in prison. His disciples take up the body and bury it, and tell Jesus.
The Feeding of the Five Thousand (Part 1)
In a desert place Jesus has compassion on the multitude and takes five loaves and two fishes. He blesses, breaks, and feeds five thousand men, and twelve baskets of fragments remain.
The Feeding of the Five Thousand (Part 2)
The crowds, filled, would take Him by force to make Him king. But Jesus withdraws alone into a mountain to pray.
In the fourth watch Jesus comes walking on the sea, and Peter walks to Him but, fearing the wind, begins to sink. 'O thou of little faith,' Jesus catches him, and the wind ceases.
Those in the ship worship, saying, 'Of a truth thou art the Son of God.' The willing hearts find land as He purposed.

Jesus declares Himself the bread of life come down from heaven to give life to the world. His hard sayings offend many, but Peter answers, 'Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life.'
Jesus rebukes the Pharisees for making void God's commandment by their tradition. He teaches that defilement comes not from unwashed hands but from the evil that proceeds out of the heart.
A Gentile woman pleads for her daughter, unrepulsed even by a hard word, taking the place of a dog beneath the table. Jesus marvels, 'O woman, great is thy faith,' and heals her daughter that hour.
The Deaf and Dumb Man Healed
Jesus takes a deaf man with a speech impediment aside, touches his ears and tongue, and sighs, 'Ephphatha—Be opened.' The man hears and speaks plain, and the people are beyond measure astonished.
The Feeding of the Four Thousand
Again moved with compassion, Jesus feeds four thousand from seven loaves and a few small fishes. Seven baskets of fragments are taken up in this desert place.
At Bethsaida Jesus leads a blind man out of the town and heals him by stages, first seeing men as trees walking, then clearly. The Lord's touch makes all things plain.
At Caesarea Philippi Jesus asks, 'Whom say ye that I am?' and Peter confesses, 'Thou art the Christ.' Then Jesus foretells His suffering, death, and rising, and rebukes Peter's protest.
He calls all to deny themselves, take up the cross, and follow Him. For what shall it profit a man to gain the world and lose his own soul?
On the high mountain Jesus is transfigured, His face shining as the sun, with Moses and Elijah beside Him. The Father's voice from the cloud declares, 'This is my beloved Son: hear him.'
Coming down, Jesus charges them to tell no man the vision until the Son of man be risen. The glimpse of glory strengthens them for the road to the cross.
At the foot of the mount a father brings his son whom the disciples could not heal, crying, 'Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.' Jesus rebukes the spirit and delivers the child.
Jesus teaches that this kind comes forth only by prayer and fasting. He again foretells His betrayal, but they understand not, and fear to ask Him.
The Coin in the Fish's Mouth
To pay the temple tribute, Jesus sends Peter to the sea, where the first fish holds a coin in its mouth. Lest they offend, He provides for both Himself and Peter.
The Greatest in the Kingdom; the Little Child
When the disciples dispute who is greatest, Jesus sets a little child in the midst. Except ye be converted and become as children, ye shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.
At the Feast of Tabernacles / The Woman Taken in Adultery
At the feast Jesus cries, 'If any man thirst, let him come unto me and drink,' and officers cannot take Him. To the woman caught in adultery He says, 'Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.'
The Man Born Blind Healed / The Good Shepherd Discourse
Jesus anoints the eyes of a man born blind, who worships Him after the rulers cast him out. He declares Himself the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep.
The Seventy Sent Out / The Good Samaritan / Mary and Martha / The Lord's Prayer; the Friend at Midnight

The seventy return rejoicing that devils are subject to them. Jesus tells of the good Samaritan who shows mercy, commends Mary's better part, and teaches His own to pray, 'Our Father which art in heaven.'

Jesus warns against covetousness with the parable of the rich fool who builds greater barns. 'This night thy soul shall be required of thee'—so is he that lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.
The Woman Bowed Together for Eighteen Years / The Man with Dropsy; the Great Supper
On the sabbath Jesus looses a woman bowed together eighteen years and heals a man with dropsy. He tells of the great supper whose invited guests make excuse, and the poor are gathered in their stead.
The Lost Sheep, the Lost Coin, the Prodigal Son / The Unjust Steward; the Rich Man and Lazarus

Jesus answers the murmuring Pharisees with the joy of heaven over one sinner that repents—the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the prodigal welcomed home. He warns of the unjust steward and shows the fixed gulf between rich Dives and Lazarus beyond death.
The Ten Lepers Cleansed / The Persistent Widow; the Pharisee and the Publican

Of ten lepers healed, one only, a Samaritan, returns to give thanks. Jesus teaches men always to pray by the persistent widow, and humbles the self-righteous: the publican who smote his breast went home justified rather than the Pharisee.

Though His friend has lain four days in the grave, Jesus declares, 'I am the resurrection, and the life.' He weeps, then cries, 'Lazarus, come forth,' and the dead man walks out bound in graveclothes.
When the disciples rebuke those who bring children, Jesus is displeased and takes them in His arms to bless them. Of such is the kingdom of God.
He declares that whosoever will not receive the kingdom as a little child shall not enter therein. Humble dependence is the way in.

A rich young ruler asks what he must do for eternal life, but goes away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. Jesus marvels how hardly they that have riches enter the kingdom—yet with God all things are possible.
Peter says they have left all to follow, and Jesus promises manifold reward now and in the world to come. Many that are first shall be last.

The householder pays the labourers hired at the eleventh hour the same as those who bore the day's heat. So the last shall be first: the reward is grace, not wages, and God may do what He will with His own.
The Request of James and John

James and John seek the chief seats in glory, and the ten are moved with indignation. Jesus teaches that greatness in the kingdom is to serve, for the Son of man came to give His life a ransom for many.

Blind Bartimaeus cries by the wayside, 'Jesus, thou Son of David, have mercy on me,' and will not be silenced. Jesus stands still and calls him: 'Thy faith hath made thee whole,' and at once he sees and follows.
The healed man glorifies God, and all the people give praise. Persistent faith is not turned away.
Zacchaeus / The Parable of the Pounds

Little Zacchaeus climbs a tree to see Jesus, who calls him down and lodges with him; salvation comes to his house that day. The parable of the pounds teaches faithfulness with what the Lord entrusts until He returns.
In the house at Bethany a woman pours costly ointment on Jesus, and some complain of the waste. He receives it as anointing for His burial: 'She hath done what she could.'
Mary anoints His feet and wipes them with her hair, and the house is filled with the odour. Jesus defends her, for she has kept it against the day of His burying.
Jesus rides into Jerusalem upon an ass's colt, and the multitudes spread garments and branches, crying 'Hosanna to the Son of David.' The King comes meek, fulfilling the prophet's word.
When the Pharisees bid Him rebuke the crowd, He answers that the stones would cry out. Beholding the city, He weeps over Jerusalem, which knew not the day of her visitation.
The Fig Tree Cursed; the Second Cleansing of the Temple (Part 1)

Finding no fruit on the fig tree, Jesus curses it, a sign against fruitless Israel. He casts the buyers and sellers from the temple: 'My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves.'
The Fig Tree Cursed; the Second Cleansing of the Temple (Part 2)
The withered fig tree teaches the disciples the power of believing prayer. Whatsoever ye ask, believing, ye shall receive.
His Authority Questioned; the Parables of Judgment (Part 1)

The rulers demand by what authority He acts, and He silences them with a question about John. He tells the parables of the two sons, the wicked husbandmen who slay the heir, and the marriage feast whose guests refuse.
His Authority Questioned; the Parables of Judgment (Part 2)
The rejected stone is become the head of the corner. Judgment is pronounced on those who will not come to the wedding of the King's Son.
His Authority Questioned; the Parables of Judgment (Part 3)
The husbandmen's parable exposes the leaders who plot His death. Yet on whomsoever the stone falls, it will grind him to powder.
Tribute to Caesar; the Sadducees; the Great Commandment (Part 1)

They try to trap Him: 'Render unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's, and unto God the things that are God's.' He silences the Sadducees on the resurrection and names the great commandment—to love God and neighbour.
Tribute to Caesar; the Sadducees; the Great Commandment (Part 2)
None dare ask Him any more questions. He asks how David could call his Son 'Lord,' pointing to a Messiah greater than David.
Woes upon the Scribes and Pharisees

Jesus pronounces eight woes upon the scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites who tithe mint but omit judgment and mercy. He laments over Jerusalem, who kills the prophets: 'how often would I have gathered thy children.'
A poor widow casts two mites into the treasury, and Jesus commends her above all the rich. She has given not of her abundance, but all her living.

On Olivet Jesus foretells the temple's fall, wars, and the great tribulation, and the coming of the Son of man in glory. Watch, therefore: the ten virgins, the talents, and the sheep and goats all call to readiness.
He warns that no man knows the day or hour, and bids all to take heed and watch. As a man leaving his house gives each his work, so must His servants be found faithful.
The chief priests take counsel to kill Jesus by subtlety. Judas Iscariot goes to them and covenants to betray his Master for thirty pieces of silver.
Satan enters into Judas, who seeks opportunity to deliver Jesus in the absence of the multitude. The price of betrayal is set.
The Last Supper; the Feet Washed (Part 1)
In the upper room Jesus keeps the Passover and institutes the supper: 'This is my body... this is my blood.' Girded with a towel, He washes the disciples' feet, teaching them to serve one another.
The Last Supper; the Feet Washed (Part 2)
He foretells His betrayer and Peter's denial, giving a new commandment to love one another. By this shall all men know they are His disciples.
The Upper Room Discourse; the High Priestly Prayer (Part 1)
Jesus comforts them: 'Let not your heart be troubled... I go to prepare a place for you.' He promises the Comforter, calls Himself the true vine, and bids them abide in His love.
The Upper Room Discourse; the High Priestly Prayer (Part 2)
He warns of the world's hatred and promises that their sorrow shall be turned to joy. Then He lifts up His eyes and prays for His own, that they may be one and behold His glory.
In the garden Jesus prays in agony, His sweat as great drops of blood: 'not my will, but thine, be done.' Three times He finds the disciples sleeping.
An angel from heaven strengthens Him as He prays more earnestly. He rises to meet the hour that is at hand.
Judas betrays Him with a kiss, and the band takes Him; Peter smites off the servant's ear, which Jesus heals. 'The cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it?'
The soldiers fall back when He says 'I am he,' yet He yields Himself that His own might go free. The disciples forsake Him and flee.
Before the High Priest; Peter's Denial (Part 1)

Before Caiaphas false witnesses are sought, and Jesus confesses Himself the Christ, the Son of God. In the court below, Peter thrice denies his Lord, and at the cock's crow he goes out and weeps bitterly.
Before the High Priest; Peter's Denial (Part 2)
They mock, spit upon, and smite Him, demanding He prophesy. He bears it in silence, the Lamb led to the slaughter.
The Remorse and Death of Judas
Judas, filled with remorse, casts down the silver and hangs himself. The priests buy the potter's field with the blood money, fulfilling the prophet's word.
Pilate finds no fault in Him and sends Him to Herod, who mocks and returns Him. The crowd, stirred up, cries for Barabbas and demands that Jesus be crucified.
Pilate washes his hands, yet delivers Him to be scourged. 'Behold the man'—they cry, 'Crucify him,' and Pilate fears when he hears He made Himself the Son of God.
'We have no king but Caesar,' the priests cry, and Pilate delivers Him to their will. The King is led away bearing His cross.
At Golgotha they crucify Him between two thieves, part His garments, and mock. He prays, 'Father, forgive them,' promises paradise to the penitent thief, and gives His mother to John.
Darkness covers the land, and Jesus cries, 'It is finished,' and yields up the ghost. The veil of the temple is rent, the earth quakes, and the centurion confesses, 'Truly this was the Son of God.'
Joseph of Arimathea begs the body and lays it in his own new tomb, and the women behold where He is laid. A great stone is rolled to the door.
The priests secure the sepulchre with a seal and a watch, lest the disciples steal Him away. Thus the Prince of life rests in the grave through the sabbath.
The Resurrection; the Women at the Tomb (Part 1)
At dawn the women come with spices and find the stone rolled away and the tomb empty. An angel proclaims, 'He is not here: for he is risen, as he said.'
The Resurrection; the Women at the Tomb (Part 2)
The risen Lord meets Mary in the garden and the women on the way, who hold Him by the feet and worship. He bids them tell His brethren the glad tidings.
Two walk to Emmaus in sorrow, and the unknown stranger opens to them the Scriptures. They know Him in the breaking of bread, and their hearts burn within them.
Jesus Appears to the Disciples; Doubting Thomas

Jesus stands in the midst: 'Peace be unto you,' and shows His hands and side. Thomas, once doubting, cries, 'My Lord and my God,' and is told, 'blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.'
Breakfast by the Sea; "Feed My Sheep"
By the sea of Tiberias the risen Lord fills the net and prepares a meal. Thrice He asks, 'Lovest thou me?' and thrice charges Peter, 'Feed my sheep.'
On the mountain Jesus declares all power is His and sends the eleven to disciple all nations, baptizing and teaching them. 'Lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world.'
He opens their understanding and promises the power from on high. Then, blessing them, He is parted from them and carried up into heaven, and they worship and return with great joy.
The Vision of the Glorified Son of Man
John on Patmos hears a great voice and turns to see the glorified Son of man among the golden candlesticks. He falls as dead, but the Living One who was dead lays His hand upon him: 'Fear not.'
The Letters to the Seven Churches
To the seven churches Christ sends words of praise, rebuke, and promise—to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamos, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea. 'Behold, I stand at the door, and knock.'
The Throne Room of Heaven / The Lamb and the Sealed Book / The Six Seals Opened

John is caught up to see the throne of heaven, where the living creatures and elders worship without ceasing. The Lamb as it had been slain is found worthy to open the sealed book, and the seals unleash the riders of judgment.
The 144,000 Sealed; the Great Multitude / The Seventh Seal; the First Four Trumpets / The Fifth and Sixth Trumpets
The servants of God are sealed, and a great multitude no man can number stands before the throne with palms. The seventh seal brings silence, then trumpets of judgment sound upon the earth.
The Mighty Angel and the Little Book / The Two Witnesses; the Seventh Trumpet

A mighty angel gives John a little book sweet in the mouth but bitter in the belly. The two witnesses prophesy, are slain, and rise, and the seventh trumpet proclaims the kingdoms of this world become the Lord's.
The Woman, the Child, and the Dragon / The Two Beasts

The woman clothed with the sun brings forth the man-child whom the dragon would devour, but he is caught up to God. The dragon makes war, giving power to the beast and the false prophet who deceive the earth.
The Lamb on Mount Sion; the Harvest of the Earth / The Seven Vials Poured Out
The Lamb stands with the redeemed on Mount Sion singing a new song, and the harvest of the earth is reaped. The seven vials of the wrath of God are poured out upon a world that will not repent.
Babylon the Great, the Mother of Harlots / The Fall of Babylon
John sees Babylon the great, the mother of harlots, drunk with the blood of the saints. Her fall is proclaimed in a single hour, and heaven is called to rejoice over her judgment.
The Marriage Supper; the Rider on the White Horse / The Millennium; the Great White Throne

Heaven cries Alleluia at the marriage supper of the Lamb, and the King of kings rides forth on a white horse in righteousness. Satan is bound, the dead are judged before the great white throne, and death and hell are cast into the lake of fire.
New Heaven and New Earth; the New Jerusalem / The River of Life; "Even So, Come, Lord Jesus"

John beholds a new heaven and a new earth, and the holy city where God shall wipe away all tears. The river of life flows from the throne, and the Spirit and the bride say, Come: 'Even so, come, Lord Jesus.'
